name: Rhododendrol

lead: Rhododendrol is a plant-derived melanin inhibitor that was developed to brighten skin tone in Japanese whitening cosmetics. It was used until July 2013.

It inhibits tyrosinase, but the enzyme also oxidizes it into reactive quinone metabolites that are toxic to melanocytes, the pigment cells. Users developed patchy depigmentation (leukoderma) and the products were withdrawn. Immune involvement has also been studied. It now appears in research as a case study in depigmenting-agent safety.

paras: It was applied as a leave-on whitening cosmetic ingredient until its withdrawal. It is no longer sold in those products.
Documented harm is leukoderma. Wikipedia reports that pigment returns in most cases after stopping, and that its use has been prohibited since 2013.

angle.text: Was sold in whitening cosmetics to lighten and brighten skin by inhibiting melanin synthesis. It was withdrawn in 2013 after reports of patchy depigmentation, and is documented here as a historical product.

lead: Rhododendrol (RD, also written rhododenol) is a phenolic compound that was used as a skin-brightening ingredient. It lightens skin by inhibiting tyrosinase, the enzyme that drives melanin production, and was developed in 2010 for lightening cosmetics, according to Wikipedia. People used RD products to even out dark spots, freckles and overall skin tone, and the compound was described as very effective at lightening pigmentation.[1][2]

Chemically it is 4-(4-hydroxyphenyl)-2-butanol, closely related to raspberry ketone, of which it is a reductive metabolite. It occurs in plants including Acer nikoense (a Japanese maple) and Betula platyphylla, and as the glucoside rhododendrin in Rhododendron leaves.[3][1][1] Early work on bark compounds from Acer nikoense reported melanogenesis-inhibitory activity.[3]

In July 2013, reports emerged that some users of RD-containing whitening products had developed patchy white skin (leukoderma), and the products were withdrawn.[4][1] The episode led to a large research literature on how a tyrosinase inhibitor can damage the melanocytes it acts on, and RD is now discussed mainly as a case study in the safety of depigmenting ingredients.[5][6]
infobox: Phenolic tyrosinase inhibitor (former cosmetic whitening agent)

paras: Skin-lightening cosmetics aim to reduce melanin so that spots, patches and overall complexion look lighter and more even. RD was marketed in this category in Japan as an active ingredient in quasi-drug products, which in Japan sit between cosmetics and drugs. A 2018 report described RD as having been very effective in lightening skin pigmentation.[2] A review noted that users of cosmetics with 2% rhododendrol-containing agents developed leukoderma at a higher frequency than users of other whitening cosmetics.[7]

RD has the formula C10H14O2, a molar mass of about 166 g/mol, one chiral center and appears as a white solid. Wikipedia lists routes of synthesis including from benzaldehyde, by reduction of raspberry ketone, or from p-coumaric acid.[1] A 2024 paper examined biocatalytic production of RD from naturally occurring RD glycosides.[8] A study of mouse-derived 3T3-L1 cells reported that RD, as a reductive metabolite of raspberry ketone, suppressed differentiation of those cells into fat cells.[9]

RD was described as an inhibitor of melanin synthesis that induced a depigmentary disorder mainly at sites of repeated contact.[10] Researchers described the unexpected depigmentation, which showed diverse symptoms, in some subjects who used a tyrosinase-inhibiting quasi-drug containing it.[11] Some patients developed lesions on the face, neck and hands where RD had been applied that lasted for years, and in some the depigmentation extended to unexposed skin.[2]

Wikipedia states that pigment returns in most cases after exposure stops, and that spread to non-exposed areas into vitiligo vulgaris occurs only after severe chemical damage. It cites a clinical and epidemiological analysis of 149 cases and says knowledge of the compound's effects is limited because of the prohibition.[1] A pathology study of 14 RD leukoderma cases and 15 vitiligo cases compared the two conditions, and a 2019 report titled its findings as RD leukoderma being different from vitiligo in pathogenesis.[12] Dermatology reviews group RD with other chemicals that cause chemical-induced vitiligo, a phenomenon recognized for more than 75 years first as an occupational hazard and then in household products such as hair dyes.[13]

Laboratory studies found that rhododendrol competitively inhibits mushroom tyrosinase and also serves as a substrate; it was cytotoxic to cultured human melanocytes at concentrations sufficient to inhibit tyrosinase, and the cytotoxicity was abolished by a copper chelator.[10] Oxidation by tyrosinase produces RD-quinone and then 2-methylchromane-6,7-dione, proposed as the ultimate toxic metabolite.[4] Human tyrosinase can oxidize both enantiomers.[14] A study proposed that depigmentation relates to tyrosinase activity reaching a certain threshold.[11]

A review of the biochemistry proposed two cytotoxic routes: RD-quinone binding to sulfhydryl proteins, causing enzyme inactivation and endoplasmic reticulum stress, and pro-oxidant activity of RD-derived melanins, enhanced by UVA.[15] Wikipedia summarizes work attributing damage to reactive oxygen species and ER stress, and notes that in some individuals a T-cell response against melanocyte markers may worsen leukoderma, with animal studies suggesting high doses are needed for cytotoxicity.[1] Immune involvement and ultrastructure in patients have been examined.[6][16] A study of RD metabolism in human skin homogenate looked at the enantiomers.[17] A screening method was published to distinguish whitening tyrosinase inhibitors from leukoderma-inducing phenols.[18]

A 2021 review commissioned by the manufacturer's research team surveyed topical, oral, phototherapy and surgical options and found ultraviolet light therapy to be the most effective; it also summarized reports on oral vitamin D3 and a topical prostaglandin derivative.[7] A second review compared the pathophysiology with vitiligo and discussed possible mechanism-based treatments.[19]

No clinical trials have tested rhododendrol as a treatment. Human studies concern people who developed leukoderma after cosmetic use, including an immune pathological and ultrastructural analysis of patients and a morphologic comparison with vitiligo.[16][12]

Treatment studies in affected patients include a blinded randomized clinical trial of oral cholecalciferol for RD-induced vitiligo, published in 2018, and an open-label pilot of topical bimatoprost on refractory RD leukoderma in the same year.[2][20] The 2021 clinical review summarizing these findings reported that UV light therapy appears most effective.[7]

RD products were withdrawn in 2013 and Wikipedia reports use as prohibited since then.[1] Its history is cited in discussions of how cosmetic depigmenting agents are evaluated, and of how the same tyrosinase pathway that lightens skin can produce melanocyte toxicity.[5][13]
